notes: cities.Rd: population estimates in 1000's of 25 major Canadian cities (CITY) for 1992 to 1996 (POP1992 to POP1996), REGION a five-level location of each city (Statistics Canada). The example plots POP1996 ~ POP1992, no model. The long form is city x year, the 25 cities a panel, not a few exhaustive series; the model is proposed, year a covariate.

frostedflakes.Rd: the sugar concentration (percent) of 100 25 g samples of a cereal, each measured by 2 methods, Lab (high performance liquid chromatography) and IA400 (the infra-analyzer 400); the page has no example. The wide verdict's evidence cites auto.arima(IA400, xreg = Lab) in the DAAG book's ch6, a regression of one method on the other, not a model of the occasions. The long form is sample x method; the model is proposed.

The help page compares two methods of measuring the iron content of slag samples, chemical and magnetic, one column each, so the long form is sample x method, sample numbering the rows. Its example fits lm(chemical ~ magnetic), a calibration of one method on the other and no model of the occasions (published_model no), rendered here with method as a covariate and a random intercept per sample. Source: Hand et al. (1993), A Handbook of Small Data Sets.

mignonette.Rd (Darwin 1877, p. 118): the heights of a crossed and a self-fertilized plant of Reseda lutea, paired within the pots they grew in, one row per pair (24). The example 'Is Pairing Helpful?' compares cross - self, a contrast, so published_model no. The pots are no column. The long form is pair x fertilization; the model is proposed.

milk.Rd: each of 17 panelists assessed two milk samples for sweetness, one with four units of additive (four) and one with one unit (one). The example plots four ~ one, no model. The long form is panelist x additive, additive the units (4, 1); the model is proposed.

The help page gives the record times in hours of Northern Ireland mountain races (2007 calendar) for males (time) and females (timef), so the long form is race x sex, the measure named by the page's 'record time', race numbering the rows since the loader drops the race names (row names). The page fits lm(log(time) ~ log(dist) + log(climb)) and a log(climb/dist) variant to the male times alone, and plotSimScat.Rd fits lm(timef ~ time), one sex on the other; no source models both sexes (published_model no). The row extends the page's model to both sexes with sex as a covariate and a random intercept per race; dist and climb are race-level covariates. lognihills, the logged copy, is not this object.

Nine pairs of elastic bands of similar stretchiness, one band of each heated in hot water and the other left at ambient temperature, their stretch under a 1.35 kg weight as heated and ambient, so the long form is pair x treatment, pair numbering the rows. The page takes the mean and sd of heated - ambient, and DAAG's onet.permutation and onetPermutation default to a permutation test of that difference, a model of the contrast (published_model no), rendered here with treatment as a covariate and a random intercept per pair.

vlt.Rd (Braun 1995): the object (one of 7 codes) shown in each of three windows of a video lottery terminal at each of 345 plays over two nights (night), with the prize. The example stacks the windows, stack(vlt[,1:3]), which names the measure values and the occasion ind, and tabulates them; no model. prize follows from the three objects, ignored. The page expects the windows independent with equal object probabilities, so the play effect should be null. The long form is play x window; the model is proposed.

Ecdat help: ACLED's 234 countries and territories with World Bank population and GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$, and PPP in constant 2021 international $) for 2020 to 2023, a lookup table created for merging; numbers from Wikipedia sit at the nearest year, as Comments note. Stack: population, GDPpc and GDPpcPPP at year 2020 to 2023; ACLEDcountry the unit. pop, GDPpcn and GDPpcp are the four years' means and ISO3 and WBcountry ids, all ignored. No model; a country random intercept with a year effect on the log scale is proposed, one row per measure in the page's order.
The second measure of row 1's stack, GDP per capita in constant 2015 US$ (GDPpcn), under the same proposed model.
The third measure of row 1's stack, GDP per capita PPP (GDPpcp), under the same proposed model.

formula: lw ~ school + iq + expr + tenure + rns + smsa + wave + (1 | person)
notes: 758 young men (Blackburn and Neumark 1992), eight variables at their first observation and again in 1980 as paired columns (rns/rns80 to lw/lw80), so the long form is person x wave, the waves the help page's 'first observation' and 1980, person numbering the rows; year (the first observation's year), med, iq and kww take one value per person. The page fits nothing. Hayashi (2000) ch. 3, empirical exercise pp. 250-256 (recalled, not read), regresses log wage on schooling, IQ, experience, tenure, rns, smsa and year dummies by OLS and with IQ instrumented by med, kww, mrt and age; the proposed model pools the two waves with a random intercept per person, the unobserved ability of Blackburn and Neumark's title. mrt, age, med, kww and year are unused.

Ecdat help: share of the US population in each of 281 OCC1950 occupation codes (non-occupational codes included) for each IPUMS-US year 1850 to 2016, household-weight sums normalized to 1 per year (Ecfun's IPUMS vignette). Stack: proportion at each year column; the codes are row names, absent from the loaded table, so occupation numbers the wide rows. No model; an occupation random intercept with a year effect is proposed. Low: an aggregate share whose yearly total is fixed, with zeros for codes unused in a year, and the occupation labels lost.

formula: ftp ~ survey + race + sex + reason + (1 | person)
notes: Ecdat help: 452 people's first unemployment spell (Romeo 1999, semiparametric duration models): duration, spell completed, race, sex, reason, search and pubemp once per person, and ftp1 to ftp4 whether the person searched for full-time work at survey 1 to 4. Stack: ftp at survey 1 to 4; person numbers the wide rows. The documented model is the duration's, with the search indicators as covariates; the page fits none on the long form, so a person random intercept with survey, race, sex and reason is proposed; duration, spell and nobs (the spell's observations) belong to the duration model and are ignored. ftp is 0 or 1 at all four surveys, also past nobs, which the help leaves unexplained.

Ecdat help: whether each of 70 countries had a banking crisis in each year 1800 to 2010 (Reinhart and Rogoff 2009), one column per country and one row per year. Stack: crisis at the 70 country columns in column order, the country the occasion; year names each wide row and is the unit. The example plots the yearly number of crises (none under Bretton Woods, 1944 to 1971); no model, so crossed random intercepts of country (70 sampled countries) and year (shared crisis waves) are proposed.

Ecdat help (terrorism): Global Terrorism Database incidents by location for 204 countries and each year 1970 to 2020; 1993's data were lost and the year is absent from the loaded table. Stack: incidents at each year column; the countries are row names, absent from the loaded table, so country numbers the wide rows. Ecdat's terrorism holds only world and US totals per year; no model, so crossed random intercepts of country and year are proposed. The counts are mostly zero and overdispersed.

Ecdat help (terrorism): Global Terrorism Database deaths by location for 204 countries and each year 1970 to 2020, deaths missing in GTD counted as 0; 1993's data were lost and the year is absent from the loaded table. Stack: deaths at each year column; the countries are row names, absent from the loaded table, so country numbers the wide rows. Ecdat's terrorism holds only world and US totals per year; no model, so crossed random intercepts of country and year are proposed. The counts are mostly zero and overdispersed.

formula: cbind(TB, subjects - TB) ~ vaccined * (Latitude + Year) + (1 + vaccined | Study)
notes: The help page's example reshapes the 13 trials to long format with study and vaccined (yes, no) as factors, but splits each arm into infected and non-infected cell counts (Freq = BCGVacc - BCGTB and so on), which no stack of the table's columns makes; the stack keeps each arm's TB cases (BCGTB, NoVaccTB) of its subjects (BCGVacc, NoVacc), the long form Study x vaccined, the occasion named and labeled as the example names it, Study unique per row. Ch_meta_analysis fits meta.MH and meta.DSL to the per-trial odds ratios and a weighted lm(y ~ Latitude + Year) of the DSL log odds ratios, models of a contrast, rendered at the arm level as a binomial GLMM with a random intercept and vaccination effect per trial whose mean varies with Latitude and Year. The same trials as metadat's dat.bcg (Colditz et al. 1994).

formula: bdi ~ bdi.pre + time + treatment + drug + length + (1 | subject)
notes: HSAUR3's vignette Ch_analysing_longitudinal_dataI reshapes the table by reshape(BtheB, idvar = 'subject', varying = c('bdi.2m', 'bdi.3m', 'bdi.5m', 'bdi.8m'), direction = 'long'), subject the row names, and sets time to 2, 3, 5 and 8 months, the stack filed here. It fits BtheB_lmer1 <- lmer(bdi ~ bdi.pre + time + treatment + drug + length + (1 | subject), REML = FALSE), filed here, compares it by anova with BtheB_lmer2, its (time | subject) extension, and summarizes lmer1. bdi.pre, the score before treatment, stays outside the stack as a covariate; missing follow-ups stay for the contract to drop.

Lowest temperatures in Fahrenheit in 22 US cities in January, April, July and October, stacked as city x month; the city names are row names, so the unit numbers the rows. HSAUR3's Ch_missing_values sets exercises on the months' correlation matrix, principal components and means under missing values, no model of the long form. The formula is the reader's: month as a design factor with a city intercept.

formula: cbind(deaths, subjects - deaths) ~ arm + (1 + arm | trial)
notes: Each of 7 trials of a meta-analysis of aspirin against placebo in preventing death after a myocardial infarction holds its placebo arm (dp deaths of tp subjects) and its aspirin arm (da of ta), so the long form is trial x arm, the arms named as the page names them, trial numbering the rows. The page only prints the table and HSAUR3's chapters do not use it; Fleiss (1993), cited, is not read. The row proposes an arm-level binomial GLMM with a random intercept and aspirin effect per trial, the random-effects meta-analysis of the effect the page describes. The counts load as floats.

housing, food, goods and service are each of 20 single men's and 20 single women's expenditure in Hong Kong dollars on four commodity groups, so the long form is household x commodity, the commodities named as the columns name them, household numbering the rows. Ch_graphical_display's exercise asks how the division of expenditure between the four groups depends on total expenditure and whether this differs for men and women, by graphics, no model; the row proposes commodity * gender with a random intercept per household. Total expenditure, the household's sum of the response, is left out of the formula.

t0 to t5 are the plasma inorganic phosphate levels of 33 subjects (20 controls, 13 obese) at baseline and after half an hour up to five hours, so the long form is subject x time, the time in hours as the page gives it, subject numbering the rows; t0, the level at hour 0, is the first occasion, not a covariate. The Ch_analysing_longitudinal_dataI slides' exercise asks for the profiles by group and, guided by them, sensible linear mixed effects models without stating one, so published_model is no; the row proposes a random intercept per subject and a quadratic in time by group, since the profiles fall and rise again. Davis (2002).

formula: cbind(quitters, subjects - quitters) ~ arm + (1 + arm | study)
notes: Each of 26 nicotine gum trials holds its treatment arm (qt quitters of tt subjects) and its control arm (qc of tc), the arms named as the page's details name them, so the long form is study x arm, study numbering the rows (the study names are row names, no column). Ch_meta_analysis fits meta.MH (Mantel-Haenszel) and meta.DSL (DerSimonian-Laird random effects) to the per-study odds ratios, models of a contrast, rendered at the arm level as a binomial GLMM with a random intercept and gum effect per study. Silagy (2003).

Timm's (2002) risk-taking study: students randomly assigned to treatments AA, C and NC took two parallel forms of a test, low and high, stacked as student x form. The page and HSAUR3's slides (Ch_analysis_of_variance) ask for a test of the equality of the treatments' bivariate means, a multivariate model of both forms that states no mixed model, so published_model is no. The formula is the reader's: form by treatment with a student intercept, a compound-symmetric stand-in for the bivariate covariance.

Male suicides per 100,000 in five age groups for 15 countries, stacked as country x age group, the age by the group's lower bound; the countries are row names, so the unit numbers the rows. HSAUR3's Ch_graphical_display exercise asks for side-by-side box plots by age group; no model. The formula is the reader's: age with a country intercept, the countries a panel of sampled units.

A wave tank subjected scale models to the same sample of 18 sea states under each of two mooring methods (method1, method2: root mean square bending moment in Newton metres), so the long form is sea state x method, the methods numbered as the page numbers them, state numbering the rows. Ch_simple_inference tests the difference method1 - method2 by a paired t.test and wilcox.test, a model of a contrast; a random intercept per sea state with a method effect is the paired comparison's model.

The help page gives each of 72 patients' weight in lbs before and after the study period (Prewt, Postwt), so the long form is patient x period, the periods named as the page names them, patient numbering the rows. MASS's ch07.R fits ax.1 = glm(Postwt ~ Prewt + Treat + offset(Prewt), family = gaussian), an ANCOVA of the weight change, a model of a contrast between the periods, so the row is a proposal: the treatment effect is the period:Treat interaction, Treat (Cont, CBT, FT) a fixed three-level factor.

Gilgai line transect in New South Wales (Webster 1977; Laslett 1989): soil sampled at depths 0-10, 30-40 and 80-90 cm at each sampling location of a linear grid 4 m apart, pH, electrical conductivity and chloride measured on each sample. The stack is location x depth, the depth by the top of its interval in cm, the three measures named by the page's quantities. MASS ships no example or script for the table, and its sources model the transect spatially (spectral analysis, kriging), so published_model is no and the formula is the reader's: depth with a location intercept, the spatial correlation along the transect left out. One row per measure in the page's order: conductivity and chloride are rows 2 and 3.
As row 1, with the electrical conductivity (mS/cm) the response; pH and chloride are rows 1 and 3.
As row 1, with the chloride content (ppm) the response; pH and conductivity are rows 1 and 2.

The help page calls it a 'Wide dataset to be used for growth modeling': each student's reading scores in fall kindergarten, spring kindergarten and spring first grade as fall_k, spring_k and spring_g1, so the long form is student x wave, the measure named by the page's word and the occasions by the column names, the page giving no numeric times; studentid is unique per row. Neither the page nor MLMusingR's code reshapes or models it. The formula is the reader's: wave by intervention (int, treatment or control) means and female, with a random intercept per student; three occasions per student leave no room for a random wave effect. Two scores are missing, rows for the contract to drop.

The help page's columns hold each participant's memory scores (0 to 100) on the factual and the conceptual questions of one quiz ('There were two types of questions, factual and conceptual questions'), so the long form is participant x question type, the measure named by the page's word and pid unique per row; neither the page nor afex's code reshapes it. The page fits no model; the flat pass cites Singmann's case study fitting aov_car(conceptual ~ condition + Error(pid)) on the participants alone (not read here). The formula is the reader's: the note-taking condition (laptop, longhand) by question type, the comparison of Mueller and Oppenheimer's (2014) Study 1 that Urry et al. (2021) replicate, with a random intercept per participant. talk, the TED talk seen (five), varies between participants and enters as a design factor. overall, the mean of the two scores, is derived.

formula: MathAvgScore ~ charter + urban + I(100 * schPctfree) + I(100 * schPctsped) + charter:year08 + urban:year08 + I(100 * schPctsped):year08 + year08 + (year08 | schoolid)
notes: BeyondMLR ch. 9 (09-Two-Level-Longitudinal-Data.Rmd) gathers MathAvgScore.0 to MathAvgScore.2 into MathAvgScore and separates year08 = 0, 1, 2 (years since 2008) off the names, schoolid the unit, the stack filed here (1854 rows with 121 missing scores, as the chapter's comment says). Its final model, Model F, model.f2 <- lmer(MathAvgScore ~ charter + urban + SchPctFree + SchPctSped + charter:year08 + urban:year08 + SchPctSped:year08 + year08 + (year08|schoolid), REML = T), is filed here, SchPctFree and SchPctSped the shares schPctfree and schPctsped times 100. The parametric bootstrap section then prefers Model F0, the same fixed effects with (1|schoolid) only, and the Notes on Using R fit model.f2a with uncorrelated school effects: variants. schPctnonw enters only candidate models before Model F; schoolName and Unnamed: 0 are labels.

formula: hgt ~ I(time - 13) + I(time - 13):I(sterile == "Y") + I(time - 13):I(soil == "REM") + I(time - 13):I(sterile == "Y"):I(soil == "REM") + (I(time - 13) | plant) + (1 | pot)
notes: BeyondMLR ch. 10 (10-Multilevel-Data-With-More-Than-Two-Levels.Rmd) drops the plants without any height, gathers hgt13 to hgt28 into hgt with time the day after planting (13, 18, 23, 28) and time13 = time - 13, plant the unit, the stack filed here; plants are nested in pots, to which soil and sterilization were applied. The chapter models the leadplants alone (species == 'L', its leaddata), a subset, and fits its final Model F, modelfl0 = lmer(hgt ~ time13 + time13:strl + time13:rem + time13:strl:rem + (time13|plant) + (1|pot), REML = T), filed here with strl = sterile == 'Y' and rem = soil == 'REM'; the text keeps Model F over the simpler Model E. germin, whether the seed germinated, is the response of ch. 11's exercise (ignored); Unnamed: 0 is a label.

boot help: populations (in 1000s) of 49 US cities in 1920 (u) and 1930 (x), a random sample of the 196 largest cities in 1920 (Cochran 1977). Stack: one measure, population, at the two documented years; city numbers the wide rows. boot's examples estimate the ratio of the two means and the correlation (linear.approx, saddle.distn, Davison and Hinkley 1997); no model of the long form is given, so a city random intercept with a year effect on the log scale is proposed. The object city (the first 10 rows) is a subset of this table.

The CD4 counts (in 100's) of 20 HIV-positive patients on admission to the trial (baseline) and after one year on the new drug (oneyear), so the long form is patient x year, year 0 and 1 from the help page, patient numbering the rows. The page states the aim, to show that the drug raised the counts, the proposed year effect; boot's cd4.nested (inst/bd.q) bootstraps the correlation of the two columns, no model.

Seven smokers with chickenpox, their carbon monoxide transfer factor measured on entry to hospital (entry) and one week later (week), so the long form is smoker x time, time in weeks (0, 1) from the help page, smoker numbering the rows. The page asks whether one week of hospitalization changed the transfer factor, the proposed time effect; it has no examples and nothing else in boot uses the table.

boot help: head length (l) and breadth (b) in mm of the eldest (1) and second (2) son in 25 randomly sampled families (Frets 1921; Whittaker 1990). Stack: two measures, length and breadth, at son 1 and 2; family numbers the wide rows. boot's examples (jack.after.boot, plot.boot; Davison and Hinkley 1997, Example 3.24) bootstrap the correlations and partial correlations of the four log measurements, no model of the long form; a family random intercept with a birth-order effect on the log scale is proposed, one row per measure in the page's order. Row 2 models breadth.
The second measure of row 1's stack, head breadth, under the same proposed model.

50 Ceriodaphnia dubia randomized in batches of 10 to five nitrofen concentrations (conc), the live offspring of each animal's three broods counted (brood1 to brood3; Bailer and Oris 1994), so the long form is animal x brood, brood 1 to 3 from the help page, animal numbering the rows. total, the sum of the three broods, stays outside the stack (ignored). The page has no examples and nothing else in boot uses the table. conc identifies the batch, so the batch is no grouping factor of its own; the proposed Poisson GLMM takes brood as a factor.

formula: pat ~ logr + logr1 + logr2 + logr3 + logr4 + logr5 + factor(year) + logk + scisect + (1 | cusip)
notes: Each firm's patents and log R&D of 1970 to 1979 are columns (pat70 to pat79, logr70 to logr79), and the help page names the panel 'five years of data from 1975 to 1979', so the long form is cusip x year over 1975 to 1979: pat the year's patents, logr its log R&D and logr1 to logr5 the five years before (logr74 to logr70 at 1975), each lag a measure of its own, as Hall, Griliches and Hausman's lag structure needs. The package holds no reshape code. Cameron and Trivedi's section 23.3 (pp. 792-795) fits panel Poisson models of patents on current and five lagged log R&D with year dummies, logk and scisect, among them the random-effects Poisson on the firm filed here (recalled from the book; its gamma random effect is a normal one in lme4). pat70 to pat74 (patents before the panel), sumpat (the 1972-1979 sum) and ardssic (an industry code) are ignored. The registry's rabe_hesketh patents.dta holds the same 1975-1979 long form.

formula: assessment ~ leader * vote + age + gender + (1 | respondent)
notes: British Election Panel Study 1997-2001. Blair, Hague and Kennedy are each respondent's 1 to 5 assessment of the three party leaders, stacked as respondent x leader, the leader a design factor of three exhaustive leaders. The page's reference, Fox and Andersen (2006), fits multinomial and proportional-odds logits of vote with the assessments as covariates, no model of the assessments themselves, so published_model is no. The formula is the reader's proportional-odds model of the assessment by leader and the respondent's vote, age and gender with a respondent intercept.

formula: score ~ test * group + pretest.1 + pretest.2 + (1 | student)
notes: Baumann and Jones's reading comprehension experiment (Moore and McCabe 1993): students randomly assigned to three teaching methods (group), given two pretests and three post-tests. The stack is student x test over the three post-tests; the pretests come before the repeated measures and stay outside as baseline covariates. The page states no model. The formula is the reader's: post-test by method with the pretests and a student intercept. The three post-tests are different instruments, post.test.3 on a wider scale than the others, which the test effect absorbs only in its mean.

Davis, Claridge and Cerullo (1997), part of a study of eating disorders: DT1 to DT7 are the seven items of a drive-for-thinness scale, which the page says is formed by summing them, stacked as respondent x item. The page states no model. The formula is the reader's rating-scale model of the item score by item with a respondent intercept, the seven items a fixed design factor of the scale.

Wolf depredations of livestock on Minnesota farms, 1976-1998 (Harper et al. 2008). early and late are each farm's depredation counts in 1991 or before and in 1992 or later, stacked as farm x period; number is their total and stays outside, ignored with the farm's longitude and latitude. The page states no model. The formula is the reader's Poisson model of the count by period with a farm intercept; the two periods differ in length, which no column offsets.

formula: employed ~ time + fin + age + race + wexp + mar + paro + prio + (1 | convict)
notes: Rossi et al.'s (1980) convicts released from Maryland prisons and followed for one year, half given financial aid (fin). emp1 to emp52 are each convict's weekly employment status after release, stacked as convict x week (time); weeks after the first arrest are missing. The page states no model; its source, Allison (1995), fits Cox models of week and arrest with employment a time-varying covariate, whose response, the arrest in a given week, is no column of the long form. The formula is the reader's logistic model of weekly employment by week and the convict's covariates with a convict intercept; week and arrest, the survival outcome, are ignored.

RAO.ASC: jaw bone length (mm) of 20 boys measured on four fixed occasions, at ages 8, 8.5, 9 and 9.5 years, citing Elston and Grizzle (1962); boy numbers the wide rows. The source states no model; its references (Goldstein 1986, 1987, 1989) fit growth curves to these data, so the linear growth model with a boy intercept is proposed.

Diggle's APTS data set: the banner calls the response a measure of symptom severity, measured at weeks 0, 1, 2, 4, 6 and 8 after randomisation (Y.t0 to Y.t8), and treat a placebo and two active agents (50 patients each); 685 of the long form's 900 measures are observed, the rest lost to dropout. The page states no model, so the formula is a proposal: week as a covariate interacting with the arm and an intercept per patient. n.obs counts the observed measures, surv.time is the imputed dropout time and cens.ind marks informative dropout, all ignored.

formula: hemoglobin ~ period * treatment + age + sex + (1 | child)
notes: 16 insulin-dependent diabetic children, 8 on the new treatment (N) and 8 on the standard (S), each with glycosylated hemoglobin measured before and after treatment (pre, post), so the long form is child x period, the periods named as the page names them, child numbering the rows. The page fits no model and faraway's files hold none; the row proposes the treatment effect as period:treatment with age and sex, a random intercept per child.

National Youth Survey: 117 boys and 120 girls aged 11 to 17 asked about marijuana use in 1976 to 1980 (1 never, 2 no more than once a month, 3 more than once a month), stored as response patterns by sex. The stack is pattern x year; count, the number of youths with the pattern, is a frequency weight, ignored, each pattern standing for its youths. The page cites Lang, McDonald and Smith (1999), marginal models, and states no model. The formula is the reader's proportional-odds model of use by year and sex with a pattern intercept.

Each of 27 pairs of twins reared apart holds the IQ of the fostered child and of the biological child (Foster, Biological) and Social, the natural parents' social class, so the long form is pair x rearing, the occasions named as the page names the children, pair numbering the rows. The page fits no model and faraway's files hold none; Weisberg (2014), cited, is not read. The pair's random intercept carries the twins' shared IQ. Burt (1966).

formula: defects ~ prebake + flux + speed + preheat + cooling + agitator + temp + (1 | run)
notes: Condra's (1993) wave-soldering experiment, a 2^(7-3) fractional factorial of seven two-level process factors with three replicates per run, defects counted in each replicate, stacked as run x replicate. The page states no model; it cites Hamada and Nelder (1997) on GLMs for quality improvement experiments. The formula is the reader's Poisson model of the seven main effects with a run intercept for the replicates' extra-Poisson variation; the replicate number labels exchangeable replicates and is ignored.

formula: y ~ trt + sqrt(month) + trt:sqrt(month) + age + (1 | id)
notes: Help page: auranofin against placebo (trt) in rheumatoid arthritis, the five-level Arthritis Categorical Scale (1 very good to 5 very poor) at months 0, 2, 4 and 6 (y1 to y4) with baseline age; the long form is patient (id, one row each) x month, y the columns' Stata stub. Fitzmaurice, Laird and Ware (2011, ch. 14) fit a proportional-odds mixed model with a random intercept per patient and the square root of month as the time trend, recalled; its terms (treatment, its interaction with the trend, age) are unverified, the companion programs not in the cache. The square root stays in the formula only; the fields keep month.

Help page: the Connecticut Child Surveys (Zahner et al. 1993), each child's externalizing scale dichotomized at the borderline cut point, reported by a parent (pextern) and a teacher (textern), the two informants; the long form is child (cid, one row each) x informant, extern the page's word (Externalizing Behavior). Many children lack a teacher report, rows the contract drops. The page names single-parent status and physical health as the explanatory variables and fits no model; the proposed logistic GLMM takes the informant as a covariate and a random intercept per child.

Help page: the National Cooperative Gallstone Study (Wei and Lachin 1984), serum cholesterol of patients with floating gallstones on high-dose chenodiol (group 1) or placebo (group 2) at baseline and months 6, 12, 20 and 24 (y1 to y5), many measurements missing; the long form is patient (id, one row each) x month, y the columns' Stata stub. The page fits no model, so the model is proposed: a linear trend in month per arm and a random intercept per patient. Missing values stay for the contract to drop.

Help page: patients randomized to antibiotic A or B or placebo C (drug), the total count of leprosy bacilli at six sites before (y1) and after (y2) treatment, so the long form is patient x time, 0 before and 1 after, id numbering the rows. Fitzmaurice, Laird and Ware (2011, ch. 13) fit a log-linear marginal model by GEE with time and the time-by-drug terms and no drug main effect, the arms equal at baseline by randomization, recalled since the companion programs are not in the cache; rendered as a Poisson GLMM with a random intercept per patient (geepack ruling, m3#22). The contract adds drug's main effect.

formula: y ~ week + factor(group) + week:factor(group) + (1 + week | id)
notes: Help page: Box (1950), rats' weights at baseline (week 0) and weeks 1 to 4 (y1 to y5) under control, thiouracil or thyroxin in their drinking water (group 1 to 3); the long form is rat (id, one row each) x week, y the columns' Stata stub. The page fits no model; the proposed growth model, a line per treatment with a random intercept and slope per rat, is Faraway's ELM model of the same rats in faraway:ratdrink, of which this table is an inexact wide twin, left to the merge's copy rules.

Counts of 32 words in -lijk in spoken Dutch in each of eight cells of region (nl the Netherlands, vl Flanders), sex and education (High, Mid), a column per cell, so the long form is word x cell, the cells named by the columns (the help page swaps the education of nlfemaleHigh and nlfemaleMid), word numbering the rows. The page's example and Baayen (2008) section 5.1.3 (inst/scripts/examples.txt) run chisq.test and a correspondence analysis, no model. The proposed Poisson GLMM follows writtenVariationLijk's documented glmer(Count ~ Country * Register + (1|Word)) from the same Keune et al. (2005): cell, the full factorial of region, sex and education, is the fixed effect. Its random-slope variant (Country|Word) would need region apart from cell.

RULE GAP: svo, the social value orientation angle the script computes from the six slider items SV03 to SV08 through Murphy et al.'s payoff lookup matrix (the arctangent of the mean other and self payoffs), is no column and no closed expression of them, so the formula names it as the script does; the script also reverses the three ratings of the attention check 'attend corona parties', recodes -9 as missing and drops the participants who always answered at an extreme, steps no cell states. Analysis.Rmd numbers the rows vpn = 1:n() (Unnamed: 0 holds the same numbers, ignored) and pivots RD02_, RD03_ and RD04_ by names_sep '_' into self (self-protection), public (public protection) and freq (how often the behavior is shown) by behavior 1 to 17, labeled by List_behaviors.csv, the stack filed here. It rescales the 1 to 101 sliders to 0 to 1 and fits glmmTMB(freqScaled ~ svo + self*public + self:svo + public:svo + (self|behavior) + (1|behavior) + (1|vpn), family = beta with logit link), freqScaled = freq * 0.999 + 0.0005 so no value is 0 or 1, filed here without the second (1|behavior), which repeats the intercept of (self|behavior). The paper's Table 2 reports a beta GLMM with intercepts only for behavior and participant.

notes: The help page's columns pair each comparison's treatment group (ai deaths of n1i patients, asp.t its aspirin use) with its control group (ci of n2i, asp.c), so the long form is comparison x arm, the arms named as the page names the groups; the page calls no reshape. a binomial response stored as events (hsame, tsame) and non-events (tdiff, hdiff) with no column of their total, so it is filed count with offset(log(same_side + diff_side)) (eggprod ruling). The four counts cross each person's flips by landing side and starting side: a coin that lands heads on its starting side started heads (hsame), one that lands tails on the other side started heads too (tdiff), so the stack makes each person's two starting sides rows, the same-side and different-side landings their measures. The page's own reshape stacks each person's heads (hsame + hdiff) and same-side (same) proportions for rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ 0 + outcome, random = ~ outcome | person, struct = 'UN'), a long form whose heads count is no column of the table. Its rma.glmm(measure = 'PLO', xi = same, ni = flips), a binomial-normal model with a random intercept per person on the wide rows, is the model filed here on the two starting sides per person, start added as a covariate. same (hsame + tsame) and flips (all four) are totals over both starting sides, ignored.

a binomial response stored as events (ai, ci) and non-events (bi, di) with no column of their total, so it is filed count with offset(log(with_days_off + no_days_off)) (eggprod ruling): n1i and n2i equal ai + bi and ci + di in six of the seven studies with counts but not in Garret (100 and 90 counted against 119 and 100 participants). Gibson et al. pooled the counts by rma.mh(measure = 'RR'), a common-effect risk ratio with no random effect, rendered as a binomial GLMM with a random intercept per study (the strata; logit by the family rule). The page's other analyses pool standardized mean differences of the arm means by an equal-effects model (as the review) and, with probit-transformed risk differences, by rma with a moderator for the measure; the arm means, sds and participants are ignored. type (intervention components) and year are unused.

The help page's columns pair each trial's reduced osmolarity rehydration solution group (ai children requiring an unscheduled intravenous infusion of n1i) with its standard solution group (ci of n2i), so the long form is study x arm, the arms named as the page names the groups; the page calls no reshape. The help page's columns pair each trial's warfarin group (x1i strokes, n1i patients, t1i person-years) with its placebo/control group (x2i, n2i, t2i), so the long form is trial x arm, the arms named as the page names the groups; the page calls no reshape. formula: cbind(abstinent, participants - abstinent) ~ arm * treatment + (1 | comparison)
notes: The help page's columns pair each comparison's NRT group (x.nrt abstinent at 6+ months of n.nrt participants) with its control group (x.ctrl of n.ctrl), so the long form is comparison x arm, the arms named as the page names the groups; the page calls no reshape. Its examples pool the comparisons per treatment and all combined by rma.mh(measure = 'RR'), a Mantel-Haenszel common-effect risk ratio with no random effect, rendered as a binomial GLMM with a random intercept per comparison (the MH strata) and the arm effect varying by treatment (logit by the family rule). study repeats for Moolchan 2005, whose two NRT types share one control group, and Piper 2009, three NRT types against nearly equal controls, so comparison numbers the rows as the units rma.mh pools and study is ignored as a label.

a binomial response stored as events (resp.halo, resp.plac) and non-events (fail.halo, fail.plac) with no column of their total, so it is filed count with offset(log(responders + failures)) (eggprod ruling). The help page's columns pair each trial's haloperidol group (responders, failures and missing observations) with its placebo group, so the long form is author x arm, the arms named as the page's labels name them (Haloperidol, Placebo); the page calls no reshape. Its example pools the available cases by metabin(resp.halo, resp.halo + fail.halo, resp.plac, resp.plac + fail.plac, sm = 'OR', method = 'Inverse', random = FALSE), a common-effect odds ratio with no random effect, rendered as a binomial GLMM with a random intercept per trial (the strata), then imputes the missing observations under best- and worst-case scenarios by metamiss; missing_obs is ignored.

formula: cbind(deaths, patients - deaths) ~ arm + (1 + arm | study)
notes: The help page's columns pair each study's lidocaine group (ai deaths of n1i patients) with its control group (ci of n2i), so the long form is study x arm, the arms named as the page names the groups; the page calls no reshape. Its examples compute risk differences by escalc(measure = 'RD') and fit rma(yi, vi), a random-effects model of the contrast, rendered at the arm level as a binomial GLMM with a random intercept and a random arm effect per study (logit by the family rule, where the page's measure is the risk difference). source names where each study's data come from, a label. Only six studies.

The help page's example reshapes the table by reshape(dat, direction = 'long', idvar = 'study', v.names = c('yi', 'vi'), varying = list(c(2,4,6,8), c(3,5,7,9))), the stack filed here, time 1 to 4 by reshape's default for the occasions at 3, 6 and 12 months and the long-term follow-up (the plot's axis labels), study unique per row. It fits rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ 0 + factor(time), random = ~ time | study, struct = 'HAR'), V from vcalc with an AR(1) autocorrelation of 0.97 within study, a multivariate model of each study's mean UPDRS difference (stimulation vs baseline) per occasion. lme4 cannot fit the heteroscedastic AR(1) structure of the true effects, written here as unstructured occasion effects per study; the known sampling covariance V is left out and vi ignored. mdur and mbase (study-level moderators) are unused. Missing occasions stay for the contract to drop.

formula: cbind(exa, total - exa) ~ arm + (1 + arm | study)
notes: The help page's columns hold each study's tiotropium group (tiotropium.*) and control group (placebo.*): the patients in total and those with at least one exacerbation, severe exacerbation, hospitalization, death, serious adverse event and withdrawal, so the long form is study x arm, the measures named by the columns' stems and the arms by their prefixes, study unique per row; the page calls no reshape. Its examples compute log odds ratios of exacerbation by escalc(measure = 'OR', ai = tiotropium.exa, n1i = tiotropium.total, ci = placebo.exa, n2i = placebo.total) and the SGRQ mean differences by escalc(measure = 'MD'), and draw them by bayesmeta's forestplot; the page fits no model beyond the forest plots. The formula is the reader's arm-level rendering of a random-effects meta-analysis of the odds ratios, a binomial GLMM with a random intercept and arm effect per study. The other end points (Karner et al. 2014's further analyses) are alternate responses, and sgrq.md, sgrq.se, fev1.md and fev1.se study-level contrasts outside the stack, all ignored. year, duration, inhaler, the baseline.* covariates and the rob.* risk-of-bias ratings are unused.

formula: cbind(out1, n - out1) ~ 0 + group * patients + (0 + group | id)
notes: The help page's example converts the asymptomatic rows by to.long(measure = 'OR', ai = tp, n1i = np, ci = tn, n2i = nn), group 1 and 2 labelled sensitivity and specificity, out1 the true positives of the cases and the true negatives of the non-cases; the stack follows it on all rows, n the cases and the non-cases (np, nn), and id (study id, unique per row) the unit, as to.long numbers the rows. It fits the bivariate random-effects model rma.mv(yi, vi, mods = ~ 0 + group, random = ~ group | study, struct = 'UN') on the logit sensitivities and specificities (escalc PLO, add = 1/2) of the asymptomatic subset, a model of the occasions themselves, rendered as a binomial GLMM with unstructured group effects per row and the group means varying by patients (symptomatic or asymptomatic) for the whole table, which the page fits one patient group at a time; the normal approximation of the logits is left out. It also pools diagnostic log odds ratios per patient group by rma and tests funnel asymmetry by regtest. study, the author label, repeats for five labels, three of which hold both patient groups (34 rows, 29 labels), and is ignored; year is unused.

formula: non ~ arm * sessions + (1 + arm | comparison) + offset(log(non + rec))
notes: a binomial response stored as non-recidivists (n.cbt.non, n.ctrl.non) and recidivists (n.cbt.rec, n.ctrl.rec) with no column of their total, so it is filed count with offset(log(non + rec)) (eggprod ruling). The help page's columns hold each program's CBT group and control group, so the long form is program x arm, the measures named by the columns' stems and the arms as the page names the groups; the page calls no reshape. Its examples compute log odds ratios of non-recidivism by escalc(measure = 'OR', ai = n.cbt.non, bi = n.cbt.rec, ci = n.ctrl.non, di = n.ctrl.rec) and fit the random-effects rma(yi, vi), then the meta-regression rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ sessions), filed at the arm level as a binomial GLMM with a random intercept and arm effect per program whose mean varies with sessions (CBT sessions per week). study ('(first) author and year') repeats for four studies that give two programs (58 rows, 54 labels), so comparison numbers the rows as the units rma pools, and study is ignored as a label. The other moderators (pubtype to designprob, interval, group, age, male, minority, length, hrs_week, hrs_total and the cbt.* components) are unused.

formula: cbind(failures, patients - failures) ~ arm + (1 + arm | trial)
notes: The help page's columns pair each trial's azithromycin group (ai clinical failures of n1i patients) with its amoxycillin or amoxyclav group (ci of n2i), ctrl naming the control antibiotic, so the long form is trial x arm, the measures named by the page's words and the control arm by ctrl's description; the page calls no reshape. Its examples pool log risk ratios by rma.mh(measure = 'RR') and by the random-effects rma(yi, vi), the latter rendered as a binomial GLMM with a random intercept and arm effect per trial (logit by the family rule, where the page's measure is the risk ratio). author repeats for Hoepelman's two trials of different years (15 rows, 14 labels), so trial numbers the rows and author is ignored as a label. year, age, diag.ab, diag.cb, diag.pn and ctrl are unused.

The help page's columns pair each trial's streptokinase group (ai deaths of n1i patients) with its control group (ci of n2i), so the long form is trial x arm, trial (the trial name) unique per row; the page calls no reshape. Its examples pool the log odds ratios by rma.mh(measure = 'OR'), a Mantel-Haenszel common-effect odds ratio, and update it trial by trial in a cumulative meta-analysis (cumul) in publication order, as Lau et al. (1992) do; rendered as a binomial GLMM with a random intercept per trial (the MH strata) and a common arm effect. year orders the cumulative analysis and is unused by the model.

formula: cbind(nausea, patients - nausea) ~ arm + (1 + arm | id)
notes: The help page's columns pair each trial's P6 stimulation group (ai patients with nausea of n1i) with its sham group (ci of n2i), so the long form is trial x arm, the arms as the page names the groups, id ('trial id number') unique per row; the page calls no reshape. Its example fits the random-effects rma(measure = 'RR') on log risk ratios, rendered as a binomial GLMM with a random intercept and arm effect per trial (logit by the family rule). study, the first author, repeats across trials (Agarwal, Alkaissi, Harmon; 16 trials, 13 labels) and is ignored as a label; year is unused.

The help page's columns pair each trial's magnesium group (ai deaths of n1i patients) with its control group (ci of n2i), so the long form is trial x arm, id ('trial id number') unique per row; the page calls no reshape. Its examples pool the log odds ratios by the common-effect rma(measure = 'OR', method = 'EE'), without ISIS-4 (subset = -14) and with it, and draw a contour-enhanced funnel plot; rendered on all trials as a binomial GLMM with a random intercept per trial and a common arm effect. study repeats for Shechter's three trials (22 trials, 20 labels) and is ignored as a label; year is unused. The page calls the table similar to dat.egger2001, with slight differences in the trials and data.

formula: cbind(responses, patients - responses) ~ arm * factor(group) + (1 + arm | id)
notes: The help page's columns pair each trial's Hypericum group (ai responses of n1i patients) with its placebo group (ci of n2i), so the long form is trial x arm, the measure named by the page's word (the column response holds each trial's definition of a response, unused) and the arms as the page names the groups; the page calls no reshape. Its examples drop the two trials without response data and one with no responses in either arm, compute log risk ratios and fit the random-effects rma(yi, vi, method = 'DL'), then the meta-regression rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ 0 + factor(group), method = 'DL') on Linde et al.'s stratification by trial size and restriction to major depression, filed at the arm level as a binomial GLMM with a random intercept and arm effect per trial whose mean varies with group (logit by the family rule). id and study each name one trial; study is ignored as a label and ni, the trial's total sample size, as a size column. year, country, major, baseline, version, duration, prep, dosage and response are unused.

formula: cbind(resp, n - resp) ~ 0 + factor(id) + treatment + (1 | id) + (1 | id:treatment)
notes: The help page's columns hold up to three arms per trial ('wide arm-based format'): arm k's treatment, patients and counts of early responders, early remissions, losses to follow-up, losses due to adverse events and patients with adverse events in treatmentk, nk, respk, remik, lossk, loss.aek and aek, so the long form is trial x arm, the measures named by the columns' stems and arm numbered 1 to 3 as the page numbers the arms, id unique per row; the 58 two-arm trials leave arm 3 empty (treatment blank, counts missing), rows for the contract to drop. Its examples turn the arms into log odds ratios by pairwise(treat = list(treatment1, treatment2, treatment3), event = list(resp1, resp2, resp3), n = list(n1, n2, n3), studlab = id, sm = 'OR') and fit the random-effects network meta-analysis netmeta(pw1, common = FALSE, reference = 'Placebo'), the primary outcome early response filed here. Rendered as dat.linde2016 is filed: the arm-based model with fixed study effects and compound-symmetric arm effects, (1 | id) + (1 | id:treatment) with equal variances, id:treatment one arm per row (no three-arm trial repeats a treatment); published_model no, since netmeta fits normal log odds ratios after pairwise(). remi (model 2), loss, loss.ae and ae are alternate responses, author a label and arm the arm's position; year is unused. dat.linde2016 holds the response counts of the same pharmacological trials (Lecrubier 1997 and Blashki 1971 match) among its 93, for the merge's copy check.

formula: cbind(remi, n - remi) ~ 0 + factor(id) + treatment + (1 | id) + (1 | id:treatment)
notes: The page's second outcome, early remission: pairwise(treat = list(treatment1, treatment2, treatment3), event = list(remi1, remi2, remi3), n = list(n1, n2, n3), studlab = id, sm = 'OR') and netmeta(pw2, common = FALSE, ref = 'Placebo'); netrank and netposet then rank the treatments on both outcomes. Stack, grouping and rendering as model 1; resp, loss, loss.ae and ae are alternate responses. dat.linde2016 holds no remissions.

The help page's columns give each study's mean difference in DAS-28 and in HAQ with their confidence limits, so the long form is study x outcome, the outcomes named as the page names them, author (first author) unique per row; the page calls no reshape. Its examples keep the five studies with both outcomes and pool each outcome alone by metagen(..., sm = 'MD', random = FALSE), a common-effect model per outcome ('The authors conducted separate meta-analyses for HAQ and DAS-28'). The formula is the reader's bivariate random-effects meta-analysis on the long form, as dat.berkey1998's page fits one, with unstructured outcome effects per study; lme4 gives the two outcomes one residual variance though their scales differ. The flat pass cites Bujkiewicz et al. (2014, Value in Health 17:109-115) for a Bayesian multivariate random-effects meta-analysis of the HAQ and DAS-28 changes on Lloyd's studies (not read here). lower and upper carry the sampling variance the formula leaves out, n is the sample size; year is unused.

formula: cbind(successes, patients - successes) ~ arm + (1 + arm | id)
notes: The help page's columns pair each trial's NSAIDS group (Ee treatment successes of Ne patients) with its control group (Ec of Nc), so the long form is trial x arm, the arms labelled as the example's label.e and label.c, id ('study ID') unique per row; the page calls no reshape. Its example pools odds ratios by metabin(Ee, Ne, Ec, Nc, sm = 'OR'), common and random effects by meta's defaults, and draws a contour-enhanced funnel plot; rendered as a binomial GLMM with a random intercept and arm effect per trial. samecont ('same control group') marks four reports whose two trials share one control arm (Aoki 1984, Diebschlag 1990, Fujimaki 1985, Zerbi 1992), which the long form repeats once per trial, as metabin counts it. author and journal are labels; year, nonenglish, medline, grey and samecont are unused.

formula: cbind(crbsi, patients - crbsi) ~ factor(study) + arm + (0 + I(as.numeric(arm == "anti-infective")) | study)
notes: The help page's columns pair each study's anti-infective catheter group (ai CRBSIs of n1i patients) with its standard catheter group (ci of n2i), so the long form is study x arm, the arms as the page names the catheters, study (study number) unique per row; the page calls no reshape. Its examples fit the inverse-variance random-effects rma(measure = 'OR', drop00 = TRUE) and the random-effects conditional logistic model rma.glmm(measure = 'OR', model = 'CM.EL'), a GLMM of the arm counts (Stijnen et al. 2010), filed here. Conditioning on each study's total events stands for fixed study effects, with a random treatment effect per study: written as factor(study) + arm and a random anti-infective indicator by study, filed as an uncorrelated slope of arm, as dat.tian2009 is filed; CM.EL's exact conditional likelihood is approximated by the unconditional binomial one. author is a label; year is unused.

formula: crbsi ~ factor(study) + arm + (0 + I(as.numeric(arm == "anti-infective")) | study) + offset(log(days))
notes: The help page's columns pair each study's anti-infective catheter group (x1i CRBSIs over t1i catheter days) with its standard catheter group (x2i over t2i), so the long form is study x arm, the arms as the page names the catheters, study (study number) unique per row; the page calls no reshape. Its examples fit the inverse-variance random-effects rma(measure = 'IRR') and the random-effects conditional Poisson model rma.glmm(measure = 'IRR', model = 'CM.EL'), a GLMM of the arm counts (Stijnen et al. 2010), filed here: conditioning on each study's total events stands for fixed study effects, with a random treatment effect per study, written as factor(study) + arm and a random anti-infective indicator by study (as dat.tian2009 is filed), the catheter days an offset. authors is a label; year is unused.

The help page's columns pair each study's pharmacotherapy group (Ee fatal cerebrovascular events of Ne patients) with its control group (Ec of Nc), so the long form is study x arm, study (the study label) unique per row; the page calls no reshape. Its example pools by metabin(Ee, Ne, Ec, Nc, sm = 'OR', method = 'Peto', random = FALSE) under RevMan 5 settings, Peto's common-effect odds ratio for a rare event; rendered as a binomial GLMM with a random intercept per study (the Peto strata) and a common arm effect. The table holds the subgroup of women older than 55.

formula: cbind(true, n - true) ~ 0 + group + (0 + group || DOI)
notes: The help page's columns hold each study's true positives (TP) of the n1 people with the disease and true negatives (TN) of the n2 without it, so the long form is study x reference group, as dat.kearon1998's to.long makes it, the groups named by the page's sensitivity and specificity, true by the page's word for both counts and n by the columns' stem; DOI names each row once. Its examples pool the sensitivities by metaprop(TP, n1, common = TRUE, random = TRUE) and the specificities by metaprop(TN, n2, ...), each a random-effects model of one occasion's proportions (by meta's defaults a random-intercept logistic GLMM), filed here jointly with group means and independent group effects per study; the third fit, metabin(TP, n1, n2 - TN, n2, sm = 'OR'), pools diagnostic odds ratios, a contrast. FP and FN are the complements, Sensitivity, Specificity, PPV, NPV, Prevalence and Sample.size derived and AUC a study-level summary; Author and Title label the study. SampleID repeats for Ujin 2021, whose two articles evaluate the full and the short-form Fonseca index on one sample of 923, a link the page does not model; Year is unused.

formula: ihd ~ arm * cholr + (1 + arm | studyid) + offset(log(ihd + noihd))
notes: a binomial response stored as events (ihd.exp, ihd.cont) and non-events (noihd.exp, noihd.cont) with no column of their total, so it is filed count with offset(log(ihd + noihd)) (eggprod ruling). The help page's columns pair each trial's treated group with its control group, so the long form is trial x arm, the measures named by the columns' stems and the arms as the page names the groups, studyid unique per row; the page calls no reshape. Its examples pool odds ratios by metabin(ihd.exp, ihd.exp + noihd.exp, ihd.cont, ihd.cont + noihd.cont, sm = 'OR', method = 'Inverse') and fit Thompson and Sharp's (1999, Table III) meta-regressions on cholr (cholesterol reduction) by metareg(m, cholr) with method.tau 'FE' and 'DL', the additive random-effects one filed at the arm level as a binomial GLMM with a random intercept and arm effect per trial whose mean varies with cholr. OR, logOR and varlogOR are derived from the counts.

formula: pos ~ group * category + (1 + group | study) + offset(log(pos + neg))
notes: a binomial response stored as HIV positive (non.pos, cir.pos) and HIV negative (non.neg, cir.neg) men with no column of their total, so it is filed count with offset(log(pos + neg)) (eggprod ruling). The help page's 2x2 table names the non-circumcised and the circumcised group, so the long form is study x group, the measures named by the columns' stems, study (study author) unique per row; the page calls no reshape. Its examples contrast naive pooling of the summed counts per category with escalc(measure = 'OR') and the random-effects rma(yi, vi, method = 'DL'), overall and within each category (high-risk group, partner study, population survey), rendered at the group level as a binomial GLMM with a random intercept and group effect per study whose mean varies with category.

formula: cbind(events, patients - events) ~ table * arm + (1 | id) + (1 | comparison)
notes: Help page dat.yusuf1985: beta blocker trials after myocardial infarction from six tables of Yusuf et al. (1985) (table 6, 9, 10, 11, 12a, 12b: mortality of short-term, IV and long-term trials, nonfatal reinfarction, sudden and nonsudden death), deaths or reinfarctions ai of n1i (treatment) and ci of n2i (control). One wide row per trial and table; id ('trial id number') repeats across the tables of the long-term trials and, in table 9, for Norris 1 and 2, so a new unit comparison numbers the wide rows, nested in id. The stack makes comparison x arm. Example: rma.peto(ai=ai, n1i=n1i, ci=ci, n2i=n2i, subset=(table==tab)) one table at a time, a Peto log odds ratio, a contrast, so published_model is no; the formula is the reader's arm-based binomial GLMM over all tables, a baseline and a common arm effect per table, as the per-table fixed-effect pooling has it, with trial and comparison intercepts. The tables are different outcomes and 12a and 12b split the deaths of table 10, so a fit of one table, as the page's, takes its subset. trial names the trial within its table. Yusuf et al. (1985), Prog Cardiovasc Dis.

formula: MULTDV ~ NCEMP * TIME + TMEXP * TIME + TMPRF * TIME + (TIME | ID)
notes: The help page states the stack and the model: the data 'need to be converted to univariate or stacked form' by make.univ with its defaults, which stack NCPRF.T1 to NCPRF.T3 (newcomer performance at three time points, in order) as MULTDV with TIME 0, 1 and 2 (make.univ's code: rep(0:(NREPOBS - 1))), and Chen's (2005) Table 2 model is lme(MULTDV ~ NCEMP*TIME + TMEXP*TIME + TMPRF*TIME, random = ~TIME|ID, chen2005.univ), filed here. ID (team identifier) is unique per row; TMPRF, TMEXP and NCEMP are team measures taken before the repeated ones and repeat to each occasion. 65 project teams.

Help page cohesion: five cohesion items (COH01 to COH05, 'First' to 'Fifth Cohesion Variable') from 11 individuals in four platoons nested within two units, a demonstration table of the package's 'Multilevel Modeling in R'. No individual id, so a new unit soldier numbers the wide rows; the stack makes soldier x item. The page and the package's tree fit no model; the ratings are the documented measurement, 1 to 5, ordinal as Likert ratings are filed. The formula is the reader's: item a design factor of the scale's five items, the platoon (PLATOON within UNIT, four in all, fewer than five) a design factor, soldier intercepts. One rating missing.

formula: internode_length ~ TR + position + (1 | TREE) + (1 | TREE:BR) + (1 | N)
notes: The OpenML page (Camacho and Arron 1995, a Canadian Journal of Statistics case study) documents the design: six treatments TR (two controls, two growth regulators at two rates) injected into ten random silver maple trees each, six to eight random limbs BR per tree (letters reused across trees, so TREE:BR), and per terminal sprout N its total length TL, its internode count IN and 'the lengths of the internodes in the sprout, starting from the base of the sprout', INTERNODE_1 to INTERNODE_29, the stack filed here (sprout by position from the base). No model is documented: the proposed model fits internode length on treatment and position with intercepts per tree, limb and sprout. TL and IN, sprout-level responses the long form repeats at each position, are ignored. Sprouts of 1 cm or less carry internode lengths computed from TL and IN, not measured, and sprouts 1868 to 1879 lack BR.

pingouin's chi2_mcnemar docstring states the design: two treatments for athlete's foot, X and Y, one on each foot of each of n people, the response good or bad; datasets.csv cites a Purdue course page (adapted). The docstring runs chi2_mcnemar(data, 'treatment_X', 'treatment_Y'), McNemar's test of the discordant pairs, a test of the contrast between the treatments and no model, so the random-intercept logit on the subject x treatment long form is a proposal (as pingouin cochran). The stack takes the treatments' labels X and Y, subject naming each row once.

pingouin's datasets.csv: 'Questionnaire rating (binary) in wide format and with missing values', after real-statistics.com. The cronbach_alpha docstring computes Cronbach's alpha on it with pairwise and with listwise deletion (as psych::alpha in R), a reliability coefficient and no model. The stack follows the docstring's long format (items='Items', scores='Scores', subject='Subj', as cronbach_alpha.csv holds it): 12 respondents, Subj numbering the rows, by 11 items labeled by their column names. Rendered as a random-intercept logit with Items a fixed factor, alpha's respondent x item decomposition with items fixed (as pingouin cronbach_alpha.csv); a proposal. The 4 missing scores stay for the contract to drop.

stack: varying=DV:Before<1 week<2 week<3 week;times=Within:Before<1 week<2 week<3 week;idvar=Subj
notes: pingouin's rm_anova docstring, example 1, 'One-way repeated measures ANOVA using a wide-format dataset': pg.rm_anova(data) numbers the rows as Subj, deletes incomplete rows listwise and melts by data.melt(id_vars='Subj', var_name='Within', value_name='DV'), the stack filed here with the column names as the levels of Within. datasets.csv: 'Scores at 4 time points', source Pingouin. The one-way repeated-measures ANOVA is rendered as a random intercept on Subj (as pingouin rm_anova.csv); the docstring's listwise deletion drops 3 of the 12 subjects, while the long form keeps their observed scores for the contract. power_rm_anova and the 01_ANOVA notebook (multivariate_ttest on the differences, paired ptests) use the table too.

formula: y ~ occasion + ave(y, species, FUN = function(v) c(0, head(v, -1))) + (1 | species)
documented_prior: gamma ~ normal(0, 10); omega ~ uniform(0, 1); mean_p ~ uniform(0, 1); sigma ~ uniform(0, 3)
notes: RULE GAP: Mtbh_model.stan mixes each row's detections with its inclusion probability omega (the data augmentation z), a row-level zero inflation outside the family list, so family stays blank (Bernoulli logit by the rule). posteriordb pairs the data with Mtbh_model (BPA Ch. 6.3, example-models' 6.3_Real_data_set.R, 'model Mtbh for species richness estimation'), which reads y[M, T] as M species by T occasions ('Grab counts' turned detections by y[y > 1] <- 1) and fits logit_p[i, j] = alpha[j] + eps[i] + gamma * y[i, j - 1], alpha = logit(mean_p) per occasion, eps ~ normal(0, sigma) per species and gamma the effect of a detection at the previous occasion, absent at the first. The data dict sets the stack, occasion 1 to 5 from y_1 to y_5, species numbering the rows; the lagged detection is no column, written as its ave() expression on the long form. The data info describes wryneck counts from 5 min point counts every 500 m along a Czech transect, repeated five times in one breeding season (Reif et al. 2008), against the code's species rows; the code is filed. sigma, omega and mean_p carry uniform priors only through their bounds.

documented_prior: alpha ~ cauchy(0, 2.5); beta ~ cauchy(0, 2.5); sigma_uv ~ cauchy(0, 2.5); (rho_uv + 1) / 2 ~ beta(2, 2); Omega ~ beta(2, 2)
notes: RULE GAP: multi_occupancy.stan models X[i, j], the visits out of K = 18 in which species i was seen at site j, as a zero-inflated binomial, occupancy logit_psi = alpha + u1 and detection logit_theta = beta + u2 with (u1, u2) correlated per species (sigma_uv, rho_uv); zero_inflated_binomial is outside the family list, so family stays blank, and K is a scalar of the data dict and no column, so the response is filed as a count (as faraway soybean). The data dict X[n, J] sets the stack, site 1 to 20 from X_1 to X_20, species numbering the observed species; the never-observed species up to the supercommunity S = 50 (availability Omega) are no rows. lme4 renders only the species intercept of detection. site enters no term and is unused. Data: Dorazio et al. (2006), butterflies of grazed seminatural grasslands in south-central Sweden, July 1997; the Stan case study dorazio-royle-occupancy is the model's source.

formula: y ~ Bernoulli(a^prev_shock * b^prev_avoid) learning model (trial); dog-specific correlated logit(a) and logit(b)
documented_prior: mu_logit_ab ~ logistic(0, 1); sigma_logit_ab ~ normal(0, 1); L_logit_ab ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2)
notes: NONLINEAR: posteriordb's dogs_nonhierarchical.stan (sic; the only dog-level model of the four on this data) gives each dog correlated normal logit(a) and logit(b) and fits y[j, t] ~ bernoulli(a[j]^prev_shock[j, t] * b[j]^prev_avoid[j, t]), prev_shock the dog's shocks before trial t, ave(y, dog, FUN = function(v) cumsum(v) - v) on the long form, and prev_avoid = trial - 1 - prev_shock. The data dict's y[n_dogs, n_trials] sets the stack: trial 1 to 25 from y_1 to y_25, dog numbering the rows. Every model counts y = 1 as a shock (prev_shock adds y), against the info file's 'avoided shock or not'. dogs.stan and dogs_log.stan (ARM Ch. 24, the logit and log models on the same counts) and dogs_hierarchical.stan (sic; one a and b for all dogs) pool the dogs: fixed-effects versions, the same row.

documented_prior: alpha ~ normal(0, 100.); theta ~ normal(0, 1); beta ~ normal(0.0, 100.)
notes: RULE GAP: culm holds the patterns' cumulative frequency, so the count of students each pattern stands for is culm less the previous row's culm, which no column holds. lsat_model.stan (BUGS vol. 1 LSAT, a 5-item test of 1000 students) expands the 32 response patterns into students by culm and fits the Rasch model r[k, j] ~ bernoulli_logit(beta * theta[j] - alpha[k]), theta ~ normal(0, 1), a random intercept per student with sd beta and a difficulty per item. The data dict response[R, T] sets the stack, item 1 to 5 from response_1 to response_5, pattern numbering the rows, each pattern standing for its students as faraway potuse's patterns do; culm is ignored.

GLM-ordinal-regression.myst.md replicates Liddell and Kruschke's IMDB movie ratings: pivot_movie expands each movie's counts n1 to n5 into one rating per rater, coded 0 to 4, with movie and movie_id. formula: det ~ date + scale(forest) + scale(ele) + I(scale(ele)^2) + (1 | id)
notes: RULE GAP: two dimensions stacked as one: det991 to det073 (and date991 to date073) are 9 years (1999 to 2007) by 3 visits, survey their column codes (loaded as integers, 991 to 73), and occupancy is closed within a season, so the model needs quadrat x year apart, which no column holds. occupancy.myst.md (after the unmarked vignette, Swiss MHB) fits 2001 only, on the quadrats with all three surveys: a single-season site-occupancy model, z ~ Bernoulli(psi) per quadrat with logit(psi) on scaled forest, scaled ele and its square, and det ~ Bernoulli(z * p) with logit(p) on date (day of year, missing dates imputed by the median). The latent occupancy state has no lme4 form; the formula approximates it by a quadrat random intercept on the detection logit, so confidence is at most medium. surveys counts each quadrat's planned surveys (2 or 3).

RULE GAP: a measure absent at some occasion: the first period's hits (Hits of At-Bats, 45 each) is a column, the remaining period's is not (only RemainingAverage over RemainingAt-Bats), so the stack takes each period's batting average and at-bats, and the response is the average, a proportion filed continuous with its denominator at_bats ignored (as hox MetaResp); a binomial fit would weight it by at_bats. The periods are read off the column names (first for the unprefixed columns, remaining for Remaining*), LastName naming each of the 18 players once. hierarchical_partial_pooling.myst.md fits Hits ~ Binomial(At-Bats, theta) per player with theta ~ Beta(phi * kappa, (1 - phi) * kappa), phi ~ Uniform(0, 1) and log(kappa) ~ Exponential(1.5) on the first period alone, one observation per player; the random-intercept model over both periods is a proposal. Season* are the totals of the two periods, FirstName part of the name.

documented_prior: lambdas ~ Normal(1, 10), each factor's first loading fixed at 1; tau ~ Normal(3, 10); chol_cov ~ LKJCholeskyCov(n=5, eta=2, sd_dist=Exponential(1)); Psi ~ InverseGamma(5, 10)
notes: RULE GAP: two dimensions stacked as one: the 15 indicators are 5 constructs (se_acad, se_social, sup_friends, sup_parents, ls) by 3 items (p1 to p3), and the model needs the construct apart, written in the formula as the indicator's stem. CFA_SEM.myst.md's full measurement model fits each student's 15 indicators as Normal(tau[indicator] + lambda[indicator] * ksi[ID, construct], Psi[indicator]) with ksi ~ MvNormal(0, LKJ covariance) over the 5 constructs; lme4 holds neither the loadings nor the per-indicator residual sds, so the formula sets every loading to 1 and one residual variance, and confidence is at most medium. The stack takes the notebook's indicator names, ID naming each of 283 students once. The earlier two-factor and cross-loading models fit subsets of the indicators, and the SEM section regresses the constructs on each other, the same grouping. region, gender and age are unused.
